Comments to authors:

This Important study provides a significant methodological advance for the study of Drosophila sleep, especially with regard to the study of its homeostatic features as well as in its reevaluation of the 5-min rest period that is currently used to define the sleep state in Drosophila. The revised version of the manuscript addressed most of the shortcomings originally identified by the reviewers. Nevertheless, they have identified a couple of issues that remain problematic, and which would need to be suitably addressed in order for this solid work to be considered a benchmark study.

In this study, Chowdhury and co-authors use Ethoscope to re-evaluate key approaches and metrics that have dominated the Drosophila sleep field over the past two decades. The first approach involves mechanical sleep deprivation techniques, where sleep-deprived flies are typically compared to controls that have not been mechanically stimulated. The authors rightly question the appropriateness of such controls, and adapt Ethoscope to provide instead yoked controls that are equally stimulated but can achieve sleep. They find that the yoked control approach yields marginally better sleep rebound data over successive days following the sleep deprivation procedure. They then find that sleep rebound data is significantly improved if only >25min sleep bouts are examined. This suggests that their sleep deprivation protocol specifically impacts longer sleep bouts, rather than shorter sleep bouts defined by the traditional 5-min criterion. They posit that this is because sleep homeostasis in flies (like in mammals) is centered on deep sleep functions, which are more fully engaged during longer sleep bouts. Finally, to support their case in a different way, the authors employ MALDI-TOF (a technique which allows quantifying protein content differences in tissue sections) to show that most of the protein changes incurred during a mechanical sleep deprivation procedure result from mechanical stress rather than sleep pressure. They employ the same three comparisons (unstimulated, yoked controls, sleep deprived) to arrive at this important conclusion. They uncover only 5 proteins in the fly central brain with increased expression due to sleep pressure, a small minority compared to the number of proteins associated with stress alone. The authors make a strong case for the field to re-evaluate the way sleep is being studied in this model, suggesting that many studies examining the homeostatic regulation of sleep in Drosophila might have been confounded by the effects of stress, or by the examining too short sleep epochs.

The main strength of this study is their clever usage of Ethoscope to better understand sleep homeostasis in the fly model. The application of yoked controls has been a standard in the mammalian sleep field and requires video-based methods linked to individualized feedback in order to apply similar techniques to flies. Everything follows from there: fine-tuning the number of random stimulations, exploring different inactivity durations to call a fly asleep, comparing yoked controls versus unstimulated controls in a variety of scenarios, including MALDI-TOF. Thus, the manuscript describes a welcome attempt at redefining sleep rebound in Drosophila melanogaster using some original or historically re-discovered definitions which are, in principle, useful for the field as a whole.

We thank the authors for the extensive revision of the manuscript, which addressed most of the shortcomings originally identified by the reviewers. This is an important study, which will benefit the Drosophila sleep community and inform the broader sleep field. Nevertheless, there remain a couple of issues that still need to be suitably addressed. That being said, this is a nice paper!

1. The main issue that is unclear is the one presented in L325-328 and Figure 2H-K. It is really not intuitive how this result is possible: no rebound is observed when comparing sleep deprived flies to rested, undisturbed flies. Yet a rebound is observed when comparing SD flies to flies that experienced partial sleep disruption. How could "sleep-independent effects of mechanical perturbation mask homeostatic sleep responses" as proposed in L327? This conundrum is not appropriately addressed in the discussion.

2. Figure 2A-D – Please note that using a similar paradigm Geissmann et al. did see SD rebound after 220s SD for 12h (Figure 5). If correct, this discrepancy with the existing literature should be discussed and referred to at ~L605 especially considering the similarity in the methodology used in both studies.

3. Figures 2 and 3: The red line in Figure 2H is identical to the red lines in Figures 3A and 3B. The blue line in Figure 2H is the same as in Figure 3B. Although this is a rather large dataset (n=82) if the use of the same data is strictly necessary, then it is important to point out in the text and figures that this is the same experimental dataset used in different visualizations and comparisons because the readers may otherwise get an incorrect illusion of reproducibility. We would recommend either putting all these results in the same panel/figure or independently repeating the experiment shown in Figure 3.

4. Figure 4A. The risk with this kind of analysis is that it does not take into account pre-existing variability. If a 3 day period is to be analyzed after SD, statistically speaking it would be better to include a longer baseline (pre-SD) too. For instance, the focal flies do show a sleep peak ZT12 of the day before SD. Also, for analysis of what is proposed to be sleep depth, we would recommend giving a chance to the Hidden Markov Chain model from the Griffith lab beyond what is done and shown in Supplementary Figure 3.

5. Figure 5: please mark on the figure what is the day of SD/treatment.

6. Line 662: "We replicated…". Does this mean that the MALDI-TOF experiment was an N=1 (one fly brain) for each condition, so 'replicated' means that a second fly was examined per condition? This seems quite thin and might need to be explicitly stated (also in the methods), with some caveats about this being quite a preliminary finding.

7. Line 576 mentions an unknown molecule. It might nevertheless be interesting to canvass some candidates, especially since this seems to have been replicated.

8. Line 617 (and elsewhere): It should be emphasized that 1-5min sleep could in principle also be 'deep', especially after sleep deprivation. This is indeed what van Alphen 2013 showed, that after SD flies descended more rapidly into deeper (less arousable) sleep, even within the first 5min. So rebound deep sleep could still be happening within the 220 s deprivation protocol. It might be helpful to discriminate between 'short sleep' which is any 1-5min sleep epoch, and 'active sleep' which can really only be confirmed with additional investigation (e.g., responsiveness, brain recordings). We would recommend that the authors use the term 'short sleep' when discussing <5min sleep bouts, and 'active sleep' only as an interpretation of one of the kinds of sleep likely to occur during short sleep bouts, especially in non sleep-deprived flies.

9. The point of Supplementary Figure 2 is a little hard to follow. Sleep-deprived flies are more active at night compared to controls, but not when yoked. This might need some clarifying, as it's somewhat unexpected and refers to a separate issue from the one being discussed at this point in the paper.

results.result: The frequency of mechanical stimulation during sleep deprivation significantly affects the magnitude of sleep rebound in Drosophila. High-frequency stimulation (20s intervals) produces significant rebound, while lower frequencies (120s, 220s) do not, despite achieving similar levels of sleep deprivation. Paradoxically, 6hr deprivation with high-frequency stimulation produced greater rebound than 12hr or 24hr deprivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 provide converging evidence from multiple deprivation durations (6hr, 12hr, 24hr) and stimulation frequencies (20s, 120s, 220s) showing that mechanical stimulation frequency, rather than sleep loss per se, determines rebound magnitude. The data are internally consistent and supported by figures. The paradoxical finding that shorter deprivation produces greater rebound (C17) further supports that mechanical perturbation has sleep-independent effects.

results.result: Using the Ethoscope system with yoked controls reveals homeostatic sleep rebound that is masked when comparing sleep-deprived flies to undisturbed controls. Focal flies showed significantly higher sleep than yoked controls despite both experiencing identical mechanical perturbation, demonstrating that mechanical stimulation produces sleep-independent effects that mask true homeostatic responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 describe the yoked control paradigm and demonstrate its utility. The key finding (C23) that focal flies show significant rebound compared to yoked controls but not undisturbed controls (C20-C21) is well-supported by data. The explanation that mechanical stimulation increases activity levels (C24) provides a mechanistic basis for the masking effect. This represents a methodological advance with clear experimental support.

results.result: Sleep-deprived focal flies display modest but significant increases in cumulative sleep over two successive cycles when compared to yoked controls, though they fail to discharge a substantial portion of sleep debt. The rebound is characterized by increased bout duration rather than bout number.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 describe multi-cycle sleep rebound with appropriate statistical support from Figure 3. The finding that rebound persists across multiple cycles but remains modest is internally consistent. The architectural analysis (C27) provides mechanistic insight. However, the small magnitude of recovery (C26) raises questions about whether all homeostatically-regulated sleep is being captured by standard definitions.

results.result: When sleep is defined using longer inactivity criteria (≥25 min), sleep-deprived flies recover approximately 50% of lost sleep by the third day of recovery, with over 25% of flies overshooting their sleep debt. This long-bout sleep shows stronger homeostatic regulation than standard sleep definitions, with significant increases on days 2 and 3 of recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 provide strong evidence that long-bout sleep is more homeostatically regulated than standard sleep. The systematic analysis across inactivity criteria (C28, Figure 4B) is methodologically sound. The finding that ~50% of sleep debt is recovered (C29-C30) and that flies overshoot debt (C31) are hallmarks of homeostatic control. The control showing all flies naturally display such bouts (C32) addresses a potential artifact concern.

results.result: Selective deprivation of long-bout sleep (using 22 min inactivity triggers) produces state-specific homeostatic rebound. When analyzed using 25 min inactivity criteria, focal flies show significant increases in long-bout sleep across all 3 post-deprivation days, while standard sleep analysis (5 min criteria) reveals no rebound.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C39 demonstrate state-specific sleep homeostasis through an elegant experimental design. The dissociation between standard sleep (no rebound, C37) and long-bout sleep (significant rebound, C38) when using state-specific deprivation strongly supports the existence of distinct sleep states with independent homeostatic regulation. The architectural changes (C39) provide additional support. This is analogous to REM/NREM-specific deprivation in mammals.

results.result: MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry analysis reveals that most molecular changes following sleep deprivation reflect mechanical perturbation rather than sleep pressure. When yoked controls are included, only ~4% of detected molecules track sleep pressure, compared to ~68% showing increases without yoked controls. Serotonin (177.1 m/z) is identified as a candidate sleep pressure-tracking molecule, replicated across independent experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C46 demonstrate the critical importance of yoked controls for molecular studies. The dramatic reduction from 127 to 8 candidate molecules (C40, C43) when including yoked controls is striking and well-supported by Figure 6. The identification of serotonin (C45-C46) is supported by m/z matching, literature citations, and replication (C44). However, only 2 of 8 candidates replicated, suggesting the need for additional validation of other candidates.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that serotonin promotes sleep in Drosophila through multiple lines of evidence: pharmacological increases and neuronal excitation increase sleep, genetic loss of synthesis or receptors decreases sleep, loss of serotonin transporter increases sleep, and loss of serotonin-inactivating enzymes increases both rebound and brain serotonin levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 accurately summarize published literature supporting serotonin's sleep-promoting role. These are appropriately cited claims from prior work that provide context for the current findings. The convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (pharmacology, genetics, receptor knockouts) strengthens the interpretation that serotonin acts as a sleep substance. This contextualizes the MALDI-TOF findings.

results.result: The study establishes three main conclusions: (1) deep sleep states are the primary target of homeostatic control, (2) multi-cycle sleep rebound occurs following deprivation, and (3) serotonin levels track sleep pressure in the central brain when accounting for mechanical perturbation effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 represent the authors' summary conclusions, which are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript. Each conclusion is backed by multiple experiments with appropriate controls. The integration of behavioral (long-bout sleep homeostasis) and molecular (serotonin) findings provides a comprehensive picture of sleep homeostasis in Drosophila.

results.result: Sleep disruption has significant health consequences in humans, sleep evolved at least 740 million years ago, and Drosophila is a useful model for sleep research. However, flies show modest sleep rebound (0-25 min recovery from 200-500 min lost, ~12.5% total recovery) compared to humans (~40% recovery).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide background context from published literature. These are appropriately cited and establish the rationale for the study. The comparison between fly and human sleep recovery (C5-C6) motivates the investigation into whether methodological issues might explain the apparent species difference.

results.result: Mechanical perturbation used for sleep deprivation produces stress-related biochemical changes even when delivered during wakefulness, and chronic mechanical agitation produces stress in multiple species.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C63, and C66 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These establish that mechanical sleep deprivation has known confounding effects, providing crucial motivation for the yoked control approach. The evidence spans both Drosophila and mammalian studies.

results.result: In mammals, sleep consists of multiple physiologically discrete stages that respond differentially to sleep deprivation, with slow-wave sleep preferentially increased following deprivation compared to REM sleep.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 accurately summarize well-established mammalian sleep biology from cited literature. This provides important comparative context for interpreting the fly results and motivates the investigation of whether flies also have distinct sleep states with differential homeostatic regulation.

results.result: Prior work has established that flies have a deep sleep state characterized by distinct brain signaling, reduced metabolic rate, and waste clearance, with longer bouts (30-60 min) being stronger reflections of homeostatic control. Flies display bimodal long-bout sleep patterns with more deep sleep at night.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C57-C62 accurately summarize published literature establishing the existence of deep sleep in flies. These are appropriately cited and provide essential context for the current study's focus on long-bout sleep. The convergent evidence from multiple physiological measures (brain activity, metabolism, waste clearance) strengthens the case for distinct sleep states.

results.result: Previous work using the Ethoscope system revealed low homeostatic rebound and no deprivation-associated death. Even gentle handling in rodents, thought to cause little stress, affects feeding behavior following deprivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 cite relevant prior work. C64 provides context for why the Ethoscope system was chosen and what previous results showed. C65 extends the argument that all deprivation methods have confounds to mammalian studies, strengthening the rationale for yoked controls.

results.result: A previous HPLC study failed to detect serotonin increases in sleep-deprived flies, but MALDI-TOF imaging suggests increases are localized to the central brain rather than optic lobes, potentially explaining why whole-brain assays might miss these changes.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 accurately cites prior work, but C68-C70 involve speculation about why results differ. While the spatial resolution argument is plausible and supported by Figure 6B/F showing central brain localization, the inference that whole-brain assays would miss this signal (C69-C70) is not directly tested. The authors appropriately mark these as implicit/inferred claims, but additional experiments would be needed to confirm this explanation.
